title: Mega Millions Game Overview and Current Matrix
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

Mega Millions is a multi-state lottery game played in the United States. A play consists of five distinct main numbers chosen from 1 to 70, plus one Mega Ball chosen from 1 to 24. The five main numbers are drawn from one pool and the Mega Ball from a separate pool, so a Mega Ball value may repeat a main-number value on the same play. A play costs 5 dollars under the game format in force from 8 April 2025, and every play carries a built-in multiplier for non-jackpot prizes.

Draws take place on Tuesday and Friday evenings at 11:00 p.m. Eastern Time, with the draw held in Atlanta, Georgia. The jackpot starts at 50 million dollars and grows by rollover until a play matches all five main numbers plus the Mega Ball. The jackpot is not multiplied. The smallest prize under the current format is 10 dollars, so every prize exceeds the price of a play.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or past-result analysis changes the odds of the next draw, and every combination in a given draw has the same chance as every other combination in that draw. The current matrix replaced the earlier 5 of 70 plus 1 of 25 matrix on 8 April 2025; figures from before that date describe the earlier game, not the current one.

Labeling note: this Signature record is Signature-original. Verified public facts it repeats are the same facts as in the public edition; any framing, ordering, or extension beyond them is Signature design, not a public record.

title: Exact Mega Millions Jackpot Odds
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

The exact jackpot odds for the current Mega Millions matrix follow from counting combinations. There are C(70,5) ways to choose five distinct main numbers from 70, which equals 12,103,014. There are 24 possible Mega Ball values. Multiplying the two independent counts gives 290,472,336 possible plays, and exactly one of those plays matches a given draw in full, so the jackpot odds are 1 in 290,472,336.

The earlier matrix, in force through 4 April 2025, used a Mega Ball pool of 1 to 25, giving 12,103,014 times 25, or 302,575,350 possible plays. Shrinking the Mega Ball pool by one ball removed 12,103,014 combinations, an improvement of about 4.0 percent in the jackpot odds. Both figures are exact counts, not estimates, and both are stated here so that older references quoting 1 in 302,575,350 can be recognised as describing the earlier game.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or past-result analysis changes the odds of the next draw, and every combination in a given draw has the same chance as every other combination in that draw. A longer odds figure means a rarer event, not a pattern that can be timed or selected around.

Labeling note: this Signature record is Signature-original. Verified public facts it repeats are the same facts as in the public edition; any framing, ordering, or extension beyond them is Signature design, not a public record.

title: All Mega Millions Prize Tiers and Their Odds
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

Mega Millions pays nine prize tiers. The tiers run from matching only the Mega Ball, through matching one, two, three, or four main numbers with or without the Mega Ball, up to matching all five main numbers, and finally matching all five main numbers plus the Mega Ball for the jackpot. Each tier count is found by combining the ways to choose the matched main numbers with the ways to choose the unmatched main numbers from the 65 numbers not drawn, and with the Mega Ball matched or unmatched as the tier requires.

The computed odds for the current matrix are: jackpot 1 in 290,472,336; five main numbers without the Mega Ball 1 in 12,629,232; four plus the Mega Ball about 1 in 893,761; four about 1 in 38,859; three plus the Mega Ball about 1 in 13,965; three about 1 in 607; two plus the Mega Ball about 1 in 665; one plus the Mega Ball about 1 in 86; and Mega Ball only about 1 in 35. Overall, about 1 play in 23 wins some prize. Prize amounts for non-jackpot tiers are then multiplied by the built-in multiplier assigned to the play.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or past-result analysis changes the odds of the next draw, and every combination in a given draw has the same chance as every other combination in that draw. Tier odds describe a single play in a single draw; buying more plays adds chances only in proportion to the number of plays.

Labeling note: this Signature record is Signature-original. Verified public facts it repeats are the same facts as in the public edition; any framing, ordering, or extension beyond them is Signature design, not a public record.

from math import comb
total = comb(70, 5) * 24
tiers = [('5 + Mega Ball', 1), ('5', 23), ('4 + Mega Ball', comb(5, 4) * comb(65, 1)), ('4', comb(5, 4) * comb(65, 1) * 23), ('3 + Mega Ball', comb(5, 3) * comb(65, 2)), ('3', comb(5, 3) * comb(65, 2) * 23), ('2 + Mega Ball', comb(5, 2) * comb(65, 3)), ('1 + Mega Ball', comb(5, 1) * comb(65, 4)), ('Mega Ball only', comb(65, 5))]
for name, count in tiers:
    print(name + ': 1 in ' + str(round(total / count)))
print('winning plays:', sum(c for _, c in tiers))
print('overall odds: 1 in', round(total / sum(c for _, c in tiers), 2))

title: Frequency Analysis on Simulated Draws
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

Frequency analysis counts how often each number appears in a chosen set of draws. The method is straightforward: collect the drawn numbers, tally each value, and rank the values from most frequent to least frequent. The ranking describes the chosen set only. Changing the set, for example by using a different span of draws, changes the ranking, which is itself evidence that the ranking is a description of a sample, not a property of the numbers.

This record demonstrates the method on clearly labeled simulated draws, generated with a fixed seed, so that the counting can be checked without claiming any real draw history. In the simulated set of 200 draws, the most frequent main numbers and the least frequent main numbers are printed by the demo. A reader repeating the demo with the same seed gets the same counts, which is what makes the method checkable.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or past-result analysis changes the odds of the next draw, and every combination in a given draw has the same chance as every other combination in that draw. A number that appeared often in a sample is not more likely in the next draw. SIMULATED DATA: the draws in this demo are generated with a fixed seed for teaching the method only. They are not real draw history and must not be read as real results.

Labeling note: this Signature record is Signature-original. Verified public facts it repeats are the same facts as in the public edition; any framing, ordering, or extension beyond them is Signature design, not a public record.

demo.code:
import random
from collections import Counter
random.seed(20261026)
draws = []
for _ in range(200):
    main = sorted(random.sample(range(1, 71), 5))
    mega = random.randint(1, 24)
    draws.append((main, mega))
counts = Counter(n for main, _ in draws for n in main)
print('SIMULATED draws:', len(draws))
print('most frequent main numbers:', counts.most_common(5))
print('least frequent main numbers:', counts.most_common()[-5:])
print('total main-number appearances:', sum(counts.values()))

title: Hot Numbers as a Descriptive Method
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

A hot number, in lottery discussion, is a number that has appeared frequently in a recent window of draws. The method picks a window, counts appearances inside that window, and lists the numbers with the highest counts. The window matters more than the numbers: a short window gives a jumpy list, a long window gives a steadier list, and two windows rarely agree on the same top numbers.

This record demonstrates the method on the last 50 draws of a clearly labeled simulated set, generated with a fixed seed. The demo prints the five most frequent main numbers in that window. The list is a summary of the simulated window, and nothing else. It is included so that a reader can recognise hot-number lists elsewhere and judge them for what they are: descriptions of a chosen window.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or past-result analysis changes the odds of the next draw, and every combination in a given draw has the same chance as every other combination in that draw. Hot numbers are not due to stay hot, and a hot list does not raise the chance of any number in the next draw. SIMULATED DATA: the draws in this demo are generated with a fixed seed for teaching the method only. They are not real draw history and must not be read as real results.

Labeling note: this Signature record is Signature-original. Verified public facts it repeats are the same facts as in the public edition; any framing, ordering, or extension beyond them is Signature design, not a public record.

A cold number is a number that has appeared rarely in a chosen window, and an overdue number is a number that has not appeared for a long run of draws. The method counts, for each number, how many draws have passed since its last appearance. The numbers with the longest gaps head the overdue list. Like hot lists, overdue lists depend entirely on the window chosen and on where the counting stops.

title: Rollover and Jackpot Growth Patterns
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

A rollover happens when no play matches all five main numbers plus the Mega Ball in a draw. The jackpot amount then carries forward and grows for the next draw, because a share of sales from the unwon draw joins the prize fund. The jackpot keeps rolling until a play matches all six numbers, at which point the next jackpot resets to the starting value, which is 50 million dollars under the current format.

The verified illustration in this record is the run ending 8 August 2023: the jackpot rolled through 31 drawings since the previous win on 18 April 2023 before the record win in Florida. That run shows the general shape of rollover growth, namely a long climb followed by a reset, without fixing any growth rate. Actual growth per draw depends on sales, which vary from draw to draw, so no fixed per-draw growth figure is claimed here.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or past-result analysis changes the odds of the next draw, and every combination in a given draw has the same chance as every other combination in that draw. A long rollover does not make the next draw more likely to produce a jackpot winner on any single play.

title: Expected Value Explained for Mega Millions
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

Expected value is a teaching tool for comparing a gamble with its price. For a single prize tier, the expected contribution is the prize amount multiplied by the chance of winning that tier. Summing those contributions across all tiers and subtracting the price of a play gives the expected value of a play. A negative expected value means that, on average over a very large number of plays, a player gets back less than the price paid, which is normal for a lottery, since part of sales funds prizes at many tiers and supports the participating lotteries.

The demo here isolates the jackpot contribution only, for three hypothetical jackpot amounts, and subtracts the 5-dollar price. It deliberately ignores lower tiers, taxes, and the possibility that a jackpot is shared between several plays, so the figures are partial illustrations, not a full expected-value calculation and not a valuation of any real ticket. Jackpot sharing matters in practice: a large advertised jackpot split several ways pays each winner far less than the advertised figure.

General information only: this record gives no advice about any individual choice to play, and no expected-value figure, however computed, turns a lottery play into an investment. Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or past-result analysis changes the odds of the next draw, and every combination in a given draw has the same chance as every other combination in that draw.

Labeling note: this Signature record is Signature-original. Verified public facts it repeats are the same facts as in the public edition; any framing, ordering, or extension beyond them is Signature design, not a public record.

    print('jackpot ' + str(jackpot) + ' -> jackpot contribution ' + str(round(contribution, 4)) + ' ; contribution minus price ' + str(round(contribution - price, 4)))
print('note: jackpot tier only; lower tiers, taxes, and sharing ignored')

title: Mega Millions Number-Pool Structure
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

The structure of Mega Millions is a two-pool structure. The main pool holds 70 numbers, from which five distinct numbers are drawn, and the Mega Ball pool holds 24 numbers, from which one number is drawn. The two pools multiply: 12,103,014 main-number combinations times 24 Mega Ball values give 290,472,336 possible plays. That multiplication is the reason a small second pool has a large effect on the jackpot odds.

The structure also fixes the chance of each partial match. Matching only the Mega Ball, for example, requires choosing five main numbers from the 65 not drawn, which gives 8,259,888 winning plays out of the total, or about 1 in 35. Matching the Mega Ball itself, on any play, has a chance of 1 in 24, while matching a particular main number in the draw has a chance of 5 in 70. Every tier follows from the same counting, with no special cases.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or past-result analysis changes the odds of the next draw, and every combination in a given draw has the same chance as every other combination in that draw. Pool structure explains the odds exactly. It does not favour any particular set of numbers over any other set.

Labeling note: this Signature record is Signature-original. Verified public facts it repeats are the same facts as in the public edition; any framing, ordering, or extension beyond them is Signature design, not a public record.

print('Mega Ball pool size:', mega_pool)

title: How to Verify a Mega Millions Result
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

A Mega Millions result can be checked in four steps. First, confirm the draw date and that the draw fell on a Tuesday or Friday. Second, confirm the format: five distinct main numbers from 1 to 70 and one Mega Ball from 1 to 24 under the current game. Third, compare the published result with the result listings of at least two participating lotteries, since a single transcription error is the most common source of a wrong result. Fourth, check any prize claim against the tier table for the current matrix, remembering that non-jackpot prizes are multiplied by the built-in multiplier on the play.

Reference values for the check are: current matrix 5 of 70 plus 1 of 24, price 5 dollars, jackpot odds 1 in 290,472,336, overall odds about 1 in 23, draws Tuesday and Friday at 11:00 p.m. Eastern Time. A result showing a Mega Ball of 25, a price of 2 dollars, or jackpot odds of 1 in 302,575,350 describes the earlier game or contains an error, and should be re-checked against a current listing.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or past-result analysis changes the odds of the next draw, and every combination in a given draw has the same chance as every other combination in that draw. Verification protects against misread results. It does not, and cannot, reveal the next result.

title: Fallacies Specific to Mega Millions
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

Several fallacies attach specifically to Mega Millions. The first is treating the Mega Ball as if it followed the main numbers: because the Mega Ball comes from a separate pool, a Mega Ball value that appeared recently, or that matches a main number on a play, has no special standing in the next draw. The second is reading the retired Megaplier into the current game: a play that claims a bought multiplier, or a prize computed without the built-in multiplier, misstates the current rules.

The third fallacy is the birthday fallacy in reverse: because many players pick dates and low numbers, a low-number combination is sometimes described as luckier, when in fact every combination has the same chance, and the only difference a popular combination makes is a higher chance of sharing a jackpot if it wins. The fourth is the rollover fallacy: a jackpot that has rolled many times is sometimes described as ready to fall, when the chance on any single play is unchanged by the length of the run.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or past-result analysis changes the odds of the next draw, and every combination in a given draw has the same chance as every other combination in that draw. Each of these fallacies fails for the same reason: the draw is random, and past draws do not change the next draw.

title: Mega Millions Compared with Powerball
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

Mega Millions and Powerball are the two large multi-state jackpot games in the United States, and their structures are close enough to compare directly. Mega Millions uses five main numbers from 70 plus a Mega Ball from 24, giving jackpot odds of 1 in 290,472,336, with draws on Tuesday and Friday. Powerball uses five main numbers from 69 plus a Powerball from 26, giving jackpot odds of 1 in 292,201,338, with draws on Monday, Wednesday, and Saturday. Both games pay nine prize tiers, and both use a separate bonus pool.

The comparison shows how small pool changes move the odds: Mega Millions has the larger main pool but the smaller bonus pool, and the net effect under the current matrices is slightly shorter jackpot odds for Mega Millions than for Powerball. Prices, multiplier structures, starting jackpots, and prize tables differ between the games, so the jackpot odds alone do not rank the games. A reader comparing the two should compare the full tier tables and the current prices, not a single odds figure.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or past-result analysis changes the odds of the next draw, and every combination in a given draw has the same chance as every other combination in that draw. A comparison of two random games is a comparison of their arithmetic, not a recommendation about either game.
